content: The 2016 Global Status Report on Blood Safety and Availability, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2017, is a comprehensive document addressing the critical aspects of blood safety and availability worldwide. The publication is protected under a Creative Commons license, allowing non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation of its content, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the work must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that the organization is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. The report emphasizes that blood is an essential healthcare resource, utilized in a wide range of clinical services. In developed countries, blood transfusions are primarily used in cardiovascular and transplant surgeries, trauma care, and treatments for malignancies. In contrast, in developing countries, blood transfusions are more commonly used to manage pregnancy-related complications and severe childhood anemia. Ensuring access to sufficient and safe blood supplies is a fundamental component of a robust healthcare system and is integral to achieving universal health coverage. Blood, while life-saving, can also transmit infectious diseases such as HIV and hepatitis. Emerging pathogens pose additional risks to the safety and availability of blood supplies, underscoring the need for effective surveillance and vigilance systems at both global and national levels. Governments bear the responsibility of ensuring sufficient supplies of safe blood and preventing the transmission of transfusion-transmissible infections. Since 1975, the World Health Assembly has adopted resolutions to prioritize blood safety and availability, providing guiding principles for the development of sustainable national blood systems. The WHO Global Database on Blood Safety (GDBS), established in 1998, aims to collect and analyze data on blood safety and availability from all countries. This data serves as the foundation for improving blood transfusion services globally. The 2016 report, based on the latest GDBS data, highlights ongoing concerns regarding blood safety and availability, particularly in developing and low-resource countries. These regions face significant challenges, including a high risk of transfusion-transmitted infections and insufficient blood supplies, which negatively impact the delivery and safety of essential health services. For the first time, the 2016 report includes annexes with key data and information for each WHO Member State. The report identifies the development of a nationally coordinated blood transfusion service, based on voluntary non-remunerated blood donations, as the fundamental strategy to ensure timely access to safe and sufficient blood supplies. Such a service must be governed by quality management principles, adequately funded, and fully integrated into the national health system. However, the report notes that much work remains to be done to establish such services, particularly in developing countries. As the global community strives to achieve universal health coverage, no country should be left behind in securing a safe and sufficient blood supply. Governments, WHO, and international partners must intensify their efforts to implement WHO blood safety strategies and improve the global supply of safe blood and blood products. The report acknowledges the contributions of various experts, WHO staff, and national health ministries in its development. Data collection and report production were coordinated by WHO headquarters, with special thanks extended to national blood programs and services that provided data to the WHO Global Database on Blood Safety.
